title: Senior's toolkit: certificate duty
summary: Request, package, automate and install certificates on Linux, Windows, Java and Kubernetes.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: certificate duty
steps.body: A week on certificate duty means CSRs, PFX files for Windows, ACME renewals, cert-manager in the cluster and a private root that every machine must trust. These are the commands.

toolkit.what: Makes a new key and a CSR in one step, with the SAN in the request. The CA signs the CSR; the key never leaves your machine.
flags: do not encrypt the key (protect the file instead)
toolkit.example: openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out req.csr -subj '/CN=api.example.com' -addext 'subjectAltName=DNS:api.example.com,DNS:www.example.com'

toolkit.what: Checks a CSR before you send it: the signature, the subject and the requested SAN list.
toolkit.example: openssl req -in req.csr -noout -text -verify | grep -A1 'Subject Alternative Name'

toolkit.cmd: openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey key.pem -in cert.pem -certfile chain.pem -out site.pfx
toolkit.what: Packs key, certificate and chain into one PFX for IIS, Azure or Windows services.
flags: the intermediates, so the server sends a full chain
a friendly name shown in the store
OpenSSL 3 uses AES-256 by default; add this for Windows Server 2016 and older, or old Java, which need the SHA-1/3DES algorithms
toolkit.example: openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey key.pem -in cert.pem -certfile chain.pem -name api-2026 -out api.pfx

toolkit.what: Gets a certificate from Let's Encrypt over ACME, proving control with a file on your web server. A systemd timer then renews it.
flags: HTTP-01: write the challenge file into this directory
DNS-01 through a plugin: needed for wildcards
test renewal against the staging server
toolkit.when: after any change to the web server or DNS

toolkit.what: cert-manager in Kubernetes: every Certificate and whether it is Ready. `describe` shows why one is not.
flags: follow a stuck ACME issuance step by step

toolkit.what: Adds your private root to the Linux trust store, so curl, openssl, Python and .NET all trust it.
flags: Debian/Ubuntu: put the PEM here, named `.crt`

toolkit.what: Trusts a root on Windows for the whole machine. `certutil` does the same from any shell.
toolkit.example: Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object NotAfter -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(30) | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint

toolkit.what: Java keeps its own trust store. Add the private root there or Java services fail with `PKIX path building failed`.

steps.prompt: Make a key and a CSR whose SAN covers `api.example.com`.
steps.code: openssl req -__1__ -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -__2__ -keyout key.pem -out req.csr -subj '/CN=api.example.com' -__3__ 'subjectAltName=DNS:api.example.com'
steps.explain: `-new` makes a request, `-nodes` leaves the key unencrypted, `-addext` puts the SAN in the CSR. Without a SAN, browsers and most clients reject the certificate even if the CN matches.

steps.prompt: Match each system to the command that makes it trust your private root.
A Java service calling your new internal API logs `PKIX path building failed: unable to find valid certification path`. curl on the same host works. What is wrong?
options: The JDK's own trust store lacks your private root; import it with `keytool -importcert -cacerts`
Java does not support ECDSA keys
steps.explain: curl reads the system store, which already has the root. Many JDKs read their own `cacerts` file instead. Some distributions link the two; containers based on plain JDK images often do not.

steps.prompt: `kubectl get certificate -n prod` shows `api-tls` with `READY False` for an hour. What do you run next?
options: `kubectl describe certificate api-tls -n prod`, then follow it to the `order` and `challenge` resources
steps.explain: The conditions and events say which step is stuck. Most often it is a challenge that cannot be reached: HTTP-01 blocked by the gateway or a firewall, or DNS-01 lacking credentials.

steps.prompt: Windows Server 2016 refuses a PFX you made with OpenSSL 3: `The password you entered is incorrect`, although it is right. What do you do?
options: Convert the certificate to DER first
steps.explain: OpenSSL 3 protects PFX files with AES-256 and a SHA-256 MAC by default. Microsoft documents that Windows 11, Windows Server 2019 and later import that, while affected older versions such as Server 2016 fail with exactly this wrong-password message; they (and old Java releases) need the older SHA-1 MAC with 3DES (or RC2) encryption. `-legacy` switches to those; `-keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg sha1` is the explicit form. Use either only for such clients.

steps.prompt: Put a manual certificate request in order.
lines: send the CSR to the CA and receive cert.pem and chain.pem
openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey key.pem -in cert.pem -certfile chain.pem -out site.pfx

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Automate everything public with ACME (certbot or cert-manager) and run `renew --dry-run` after any web or DNS change: with lifetimes heading to 47 days, manual renewal is an outage waiting to happen. Keep a short runbook of the trust commands for each platform your company runs, including Java.
